title: Rhetoric and debate
note: Aristotle named three technical means of persuasion: ethos, the speaker's character as shown in the speech; pathos, the hearers' emotions; and logos, the argument itself. In fair debate, whoever makes a claim bears the burden of proof, objections aim at the strongest version of a view, and questions expose hidden assumptions.

read.title: Persuading fairly
text: Aristotle defined rhetoric as the ability to see the available means of persuasion in each case. He named three that the speaker supplies. Ethos is the speaker's character as it comes across in the speech: good sense, good will, and virtue. Pathos is putting the audience in a fitting frame of mind. Logos is the argument itself, and Aristotle considered the enthymeme, a deduction from premises the audience already accepts, the 'body' of persuasion.

None of these is a trick in itself. Emotion is fitting when the facts warrant it, and a speaker's track record is real evidence. They become manipulation when they replace reasons rather than accompany them.

Fair debate has rules of its own. Whoever makes a claim carries the burden of proof; demanding that others disprove it shifts that burden unfairly. Socrates showed the power of questions: by drawing out what a person already believed, he exposed contradictions and left the confident puzzled, a state called aporia.

Good refutation aims at the strongest form of a view. One clear counterexample can refute a universal claim, and showing that a view implies something absurd can refute it outright. Conceding what is true in an opponent's case usually makes your remaining objections more credible.
